info.title: Nyquist
info.text: To record a sound accurately you must sample at least twice its highest frequency. Human hearing reaches about 20 kHz, hence 44.1 kHz on CDs.

info.title: Bit depth and noise
info.text: Low bit depth adds a hiss called quantisation noise, because each sample is rounded to the nearest level.

info.title: MP3
info.text: MP3 files are much smaller than CD audio because they throw away sounds most people can't hear: that's lossy compression, in lesson 15.

info.title: Studio quality
info.text: Music studios record at 96 kHz or higher with 24-bit depth, giving huge files that are mixed down later.

info.title: Telephone bandwidth
info.text: Phone systems keep only 300 Hz to 3,400 Hz, which is why voices sound thinner on a call than in person.

info.title: Vinyl is analogue
info.text: A record groove is a physical copy of the wave, with no sampling at all: that's what people mean by analogue sound.
